topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on middle school education level, but geographic scope and specific curriculum context are unclear from title and snippet. Applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development requires further assessment.
takeaways: AI competencies should be embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation, helping learners see connections between AI, data literacy, and critical thinking.
A holistic approach to AI education for younger learners may establish foundational understanding that supports more advanced AI capability development in adult professional settings.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on public health faculty development; findings may apply to other academic disciplines but sector-specific context limits broader generalisation. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption can be systematically reduced through structured development programs that build confidence and competence before requiring implementation.
Designing AI literacy initiatives for educators (rather than only students) creates a multiplier effect—trained faculty can then teach AI literacy more effectively across their institutions.
Addressing mindset barriers through targeted professional development is as important as technical training when introducing AI to established workforces.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; frameworks and competencies may have limited direct applicability to Australian workplace AI literacy programmes, though core digital competency principles are likely transferable.
takeaways: Identify which digital and AI competencies are most critical for your workforce by mapping against established European public health frameworks—this ensures training aligns with evidence-based skill hierarchies rather than ad-hoc capability gaps.

Design competency assessments that span technical, data literacy, and change-management skills, not just technical AI knowledge—public health experience shows balanced competency development improves adoption and implementation success.
Use scoping review findings to benchmark your organisation's current AI capability maturity against European standards, helping prioritise upskilling efforts where gaps are greatest.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's global client base and research, but skewed toward large organisations and developed economies. Findings may not reflect priorities in small-to-medium enterprises or resource-constrained sectors.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation will be most disrupted by gen AI (e.g. data entry, basic analysis, content creation) and prioritise upskilling pathways for those employee populations first.

Design reskilling programs that pair technical AI literacy (prompt engineering, AI tool use) with complementary soft skills (critical thinking, creativity, complex problem-solving) rather than technical training alone.

Audit your current learning infrastructure and consider whether existing internal training can be adapted for AI capabilities or whether you need to partner with external providers or leverage platforms like LinkedIn Learning or Coursera for at-scale delivery.

articles.title: Development and influencing factors of artificial intelligence literacy and computational thinking in Chinese university students - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and influencing factors of artificial intelligence literacy and computational thinking in Chinese university students  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to Chinese higher education context. Findings on AI literacy development and computational thinking may reflect curriculum structures, educational policies, and student demographics specific to Chinese universities and may not generalise to Australian or Western educational systems.
takeaways: Identify which factors most strongly predict AI literacy development in your student or employee cohort (e.g., prior computational thinking skills, domain background, motivation) — the study's influencing factors can guide targeted upskilling interventions.
Consider whether computational thinking should be a prerequisite or parallel pathway in AI literacy programs, rather than assuming AI knowledge alone is sufficient for capability development.

articles.title: Fostering AI literacy in pre-service teachers: impact of a training intervention on awareness, attitude and trust in AI - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Fostering AI literacy in pre-service teachers: impact of a training intervention on awareness, attitude and trust in AI  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings apply to pre-service teacher populations, but generalisability to working professionals in non-education sectors is limited. Geographic scope not clearly indicated from title/snippet.
takeaways: Structured AI literacy training can measurably shift attitudes and trust in AI among learners; consider designing comparable interventions for your employee cohorts to move beyond passive awareness to active comfort with AI tools.

Pre-service teachers' receptiveness to AI training suggests that earlier, developmental approaches to AI literacy may be more effective than remedial upskilling of experienced workers — consider the timing and framing of AI capability programs in your organisation.

Tracking awareness, attitude, and trust as separate outcomes reveals that knowledge alone doesn't build trust; design interventions that explicitly address psychological and emotional barriers to AI adoption, not just technical knowledge.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess without access to full article — title suggests a theoretical or empirical examination of AI adoption effects, but sample characteristics, geography, and methodology are unclear from the snippet provided.
takeaways: AI adoption in organizations can have both positive and negative effects on employee creativity; implementation strategies should account for potential downsides (e.g., over-reliance on AI suggestions, reduced divergent thinking) alongside benefits.

When rolling out AI tools, monitor how they shape creative work processes — some employees may become more efficient while others may experience diminished autonomy or intrinsic motivation to innovate independently.

articles.title: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not detailed in snippet. The dual-pathway model may apply across sectors, but effectiveness likely varies by organisation size, industry, and implementation approach.
takeaways: Design AI capability-building programmes that simultaneously address anxiety and job insecurity — treating these as linked psychological outcomes rather than separate concerns will improve employee engagement with transformation initiatives.

Use the dual-pathway model to identify whether your organisation is creating employee empowerment (positive pathway) or anxiety/insecurity (negative pathway) — measure both capability gains AND psychological safety to assess true transformation success.

Prioritise upskilling and clear role reframing before AI deployment to shift employees from threat perception toward capability development, reducing resistance and supporting sustainable organisational change.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics, which are not detailed in the snippet. The focus on paternalistic leadership suggests potential limitations to organisational contexts where this leadership style is prevalent, possibly more relevant in hierarchical cultures.
takeaways: Fostering psychological ownership of AI tools among employees — the sense that they 'own' the technology — can increase their willingness to actively collaborate with and shape AI systems rather than passively accept them.

AI crafting (customising or modifying AI tools to fit individual work) appears to be a key mechanism linking ownership to collaboration; consider designing workflows that allow employees to personalise AI workflows to their role.

Leadership style matters: paternalistic leaders (who show personal concern while maintaining authority) may be particularly effective at driving this ownership and crafting behaviour, suggesting that leader communication about AI adoption should balance guidance with employee agency.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings; may have limited applicability to Australian workplace context due to differences in employment law, union representation, and social safety nets. Psychological principles around uncertainty may have broader relevance.
takeaways: Acknowledge that AI-driven workplace uncertainty affects employee wellbeing and psychological safety — create explicit channels for staff to voice concerns about automation and role changes without fear of retaliation.
Provide transparent communication about how AI will be implemented and what skills will remain valued; uncertainty itself is often more damaging to morale than the change itself.

Build resilience and adaptability skills through development programs that help workers see AI as a tool they can learn to use, rather than a threat — this shifts the narrative from loss to opportunity.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample characteristics, which are not evident from the title and snippet alone. The finding that AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health via reduced psychological safety is likely relevant across sectors, but geographic scope and sample diversity are unclear.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical mediator in the AI adoption–employee wellbeing relationship; leaders should actively foster safe spaces for questions and concerns about AI implementation to protect mental health.

Ethical leadership during AI rollout is essential—employees experiencing AI-related stress require transparent communication about how AI decisions are made and assurance that human values guide implementation.

Monitor employee depression and psychological wellbeing indicators closely during AI adoption phases, particularly among staff whose roles are most affected, to identify and mitigate negative mental health impacts early.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition, which are not detailed in the snippet. The theoretical framework (approach-avoidance perspective) may apply across sectors, but geographic scope and organisational context are unclear.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger different emotional and behavioural responses in employees — some may actively reshape their roles (approach) while others may withdraw or resist (avoidance); understanding which factors drive each response helps tailor change management strategies.

Employees' job crafting behaviours during AI implementation may reflect their psychological comfort with technology and perceived job security; interventions that address anxiety and clarify how AI will change (not eliminate) their roles can shift responses toward constructive adaptation.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte's framework is based on consulting experience but lacks transparent methodology, sample details, or peer review. Applicability depends on organisational context and sector.
takeaways: Shift from 'adoption' framing (compliance-focused) to 'adaptation' framing (capability-building) to encourage employees to develop new behaviours rather than simply comply with AI tools.

Design change initiatives that explicitly target the human behaviours needed for AI use — such as critical evaluation, prompt engineering, and cross-functional collaboration — rather than focusing solely on technical training.
Use staged, iterative approaches that allow employees to experiment with AI in low-stakes environments before full-scale deployment, reducing resistance and building confidence in AI-augmented work.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — likely limited by sample characteristics and organisational context not detailed in the provided information. Geographic scope not stated.
takeaways: Employees may respond to AI adoption through job crafting — either seeking opportunities to work with AI tools (approach) or withdrawing from AI-related tasks (avoidance). Understanding which employees gravitate toward which response helps target support and upskilling.

Recognition that AI adoption triggers psychological approach-avoidance conflict suggests organisations should address both fear and opportunity simultaneously — not just promoting AI benefits, but also validating concerns and providing safe spaces to experiment.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reflects BCG's client base and consulting experience, likely skewed toward large organisations and developed economies. Findings may not generalise to small/medium enterprises or resource-constrained settings.
takeaways: Workforce transformation must accompany AI adoption; technical implementation alone will fail without concurrent changes to roles, skills, and team structures.
Develop a clear change management strategy that addresses employee concerns, redefines job responsibilities, and creates pathways for reskilling before rolling out AI tools.
Prioritise early communication and involvement of frontline teams in AI implementation planning to build buy-in and reduce resistance to behaviour and process changes.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical scope or geographic focus. Insights may reflect US higher education and business school perspectives.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation are most exposed to AI-driven change, then design targeted upskilling programmes before disruption occurs rather than reacting after.

Create psychological safety around AI adoption by explicitly acknowledging workforce concerns about displacement; frame AI as a tool augmenting roles rather than replacing workers, and communicate this consistently through leadership.
Map your organisation's current AI readiness gaps (skills, culture, processes) now — waiting for external pressure to change behaviour typically creates resistance and delays adaptation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited by lack of geographic and sector specification in the snippet. Findings may not generalize across all organizational contexts, regions, or AI implementation types without access to full methodology.
takeaways: When introducing AI, explicitly prioritize psychological safety and ethical leadership practices — their absence appears to mediate increased depression risk among employees, suggesting these are critical protective factors during technological transitions.

Monitor employee mental health during AI adoption as a key performance indicator; depression linked to poor AI implementation signals leaders need to reassess communication transparency, involvement in decision-making, and clarity around ethical AI use.

Frame AI adoption conversations around ethical leadership and psychological safety from the outset rather than treating these as secondary concerns — they appear to be primary levers that determine whether AI integration supports or harms employee wellbeing.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey insights draw on consulting experience across sectors and geographies, but findings reflect client organisations that engage premium consulting and may skew toward large enterprises; smaller or under-resourced organisations may face different barriers.
takeaways: Structure AI transformation in phases (adoption → scaling → sustained impact) rather than treating it as a single event; this helps teams realistic about timelines and resource needs for behaviour change across the organisation.

Identify which 'horizon' your organisation is in before designing capability-building interventions; early-stage adopters need different support (foundational literacy, pilot mindset) than organisations scaling AI across operations (change management, role redesign).

Anchor AI change initiatives to measurable business outcomes from the start, not just technology deployment; this clarifies why behaviour and practice change matter and helps secure sustained leadership buy-in.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — draws on established psychological research across multiple studies and populations, though specific mechanisms may vary by cultural context.
takeaways: Close friendships appear to have measurable health benefits comparable to or exceeding major lifestyle factors like exercise and diet — a counterintuitive finding that challenges how we prioritise wellbeing.

Social connection works through multiple biological pathways: stress reduction, immune system boosting, and cardiovascular protection — meaning friendship is literally protective medicine for your body.
The quality and depth of friendships matters far more than quantity; a few genuine relationships outperform large but shallow social networks for health outcomes.

articles.title: Personality traits in musicians with different types of music performance anxiety - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Personality traits in musicians with different types of music performance anxiety  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — sample size and geographic scope unclear from snippet; findings may not generalise beyond the specific musician population studied.
takeaways: Musicians experience distinct patterns of performance anxiety tied to their personality profiles, suggesting anxiety isn't one-size-fits-all even within the same profession.
The link between personality traits and how musicians experience performance pressure reveals why two musicians might choke in completely different ways during the same performance.
Understanding personality-anxiety profiles could explain why some musicians thrive under pressure while others struggle, even with equal technical skill and experience.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely high — suggests cross-cultural patterns in music and personality, though specific sample details would affect confidence in global applicability.
takeaways: People with similar personality traits tend to like similar music across different cultures — your taste in music genuinely reveals something universal about who you are, not just your background.

This challenges the idea that musical preferences are purely cultural; there's a personality signal buried in your Spotify playlist that would probably resonate with someone on the other side of the world with the same traits.
It's a neat counterpoint to the assumption that everything about taste is local — turns out what you listen to might say more about your temperament than your ZIP code.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Moderate — a psychological perspectives review likely draws on international research but scope depends on included studies; specific geographic representation unclear from title and snippet.
takeaways: True crime's appeal isn't morbid curiosity — psychological research suggests it satisfies needs for control, safety understanding, and narrative closure that everyday life doesn't provide.

The genre attracts diverse audiences for different reasons: some seek threat simulation and risk assessment skills, others pursue parasocial connection or justice-system understanding — not a one-size-fits-all explanation.
True crime consumption is surprisingly mainstream and psychologically normal, reflecting how humans use storytelling to process fear and danger in a controlled, low-stakes environment.

articles.title: How dogs think - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How dogs think  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a brief overview or commentary rather than a systematic synthesis of evidence. Specific research backing claims is not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Dogs likely process information differently from humans in ways that surprise us — they may not think about the world the way we assume they do.
Understanding canine cognition reveals how evolution shapes perception and problem-solving, which is fascinating regardless of species.
This topic bridges animal behaviour science with everyday pet ownership, making cognitive science relatable and entertaining for general audiences.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews existing research on MBTI's predictive validity, but findings depend on quality and scope of underlying studies reviewed.
takeaways: Despite its ubiquitous use in organisational settings, the MBTI has surprisingly weak empirical support for predicting actual leadership behaviours — a counterintuitive gap between popularity and scientific evidence.

The findings highlight a common human bias: we love personality frameworks because they're intuitive and flattering, even when rigorous research suggests they don't predict real-world outcomes as well as we'd hope.

This mismatch is a fascinating case study in why organisations stick with beloved tools despite weak evidence — and a reminder to question whether your favourite team assessment tool is actually measuring what it claims.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate — large global sample, but PwC survey methodology and respondent characteristics not detailed in snippet; findings may skew toward larger organisations and sectors where PwC operates.
takeaways: Identify which workforce fears (job security, skills obsolescence, AI displacement) are most acute in your organisation by benchmarking against global trends—this reveals psychological safety gaps to address.
Use PwC's global data on employee hopes to design targeted interventions: if hope for career development is low, strengthen transparent upskilling pathways and mentoring to rebuild trust and safety.

Track year-on-year shifts in hopes vs. fears to assess whether your psych safety initiatives are moving the needle—improvements in employee confidence about the future signal stronger psychological safety.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and size, which are not detailed in the snippet. The relationship between AI adoption, psychological safety, and employee mental health may vary significantly by industry, organisational culture, and implementation approach.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical mediator in how AI adoption affects employee wellbeing — organisations rolling out AI should actively cultivate trust and openness to mitigate depressive symptoms rather than assuming technical implementation alone is sufficient.

Ethical leadership during AI adoption is protective; leaders who model transparency, fairness, and accountability when introducing AI systems help employees feel safer and less distressed about technological change.

Monitor employee mental health outcomes explicitly during and after AI implementation, rather than assuming adoption is a neutral or positive change — depression risk is real and preventable through deliberate cultural and leadership interventions.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's insights draw on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition, methodology, and geographic focus are unclear from the snippet alone.
takeaways: Creating psychological safety actively reduces barriers to participation for underrepresented or quieter employees, enabling more diverse voices and perspectives to contribute in meetings and decision-making.

Leaders can level the playing field by establishing clear norms that reward asking questions and admitting mistakes, which signals that all employees—regardless of seniority or background—have permission to speak up without fear of embarrassment or retaliation.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused survey data — findings reflect American workplace conditions, employment law, and cultural contexts that may not directly transfer to Australian organisations, though core psychological safety principles are likely universal.
takeaways: Assess your team's current psychological safety baseline using validated measures (e.g., Edmondson's scale) to identify specific gaps — silence around mistakes, fear of speaking up in meetings, or reluctance to ask for help — rather than assuming uniform safety across the organisation.

Link psychological safety explicitly to business outcomes relevant to your context (retention, innovation, mental health) when building the case for interventions with leadership, as generic 'well-being' framing often fails to secure resources.

Start with leader behaviour change — research consistently shows that manager vulnerability, encouraging questions, and responsive listening are the strongest drivers of psychological safety, so focus first on coaching managers rather than team-level interventions alone.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but lacks peer-reviewed validation and specific sample details. Findings likely most applicable to large organisations with resources to implement comprehensive AI adoption programmes.
takeaways: Create clear role definitions and decision-making authority for employees working with AI systems—'superagency' requires people to understand which decisions they own and which require human oversight, reducing ambiguity and psychological safety violations.

Invest in transparent communication about AI capabilities and limitations upfront; employees are more likely to engage confidently with AI tools when they understand what the system can and cannot do, rather than discovering constraints through failure.

Design feedback loops and safe-to-fail environments where employees can experiment with AI without fear of punishment, enabling psychological safety and building collective AI capability over time rather than relying on isolated 'AI champions'.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM content is US-focused and draws on established psychological safety research, but specific organisational context and applicability to Australian workplaces not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Identify the four specific leader behaviours SHRM recommends (likely including modelling vulnerability, inviting input, responding constructively to concerns, and holding people accountable fairly) and assess which are weakest in your current team or organisation.

Use this as a diagnostic tool: survey your team on their sense of psychological safety and cross-reference gaps against the four ways leaders can build it, then prioritise the behaviour shift that will have most impact.
Note that SHRM guidance is primarily US-based; adapt recommendations to Australian employment context, workplace culture norms, and your industry's specific safety and feedback practices.
